text: Lesson 3 found specific session IDs with unusually high total elapsed time. That's a start, but a session ID alone doesn't tell you what query actually ran. sys dot dm_exec_query_stats has the answer: cumulative execution statistics for every plan sitting in the plan cache, accumulated since that plan was compiled.

This query ranks every cached plan by total CPU time consumed — the worst offenders, sourced live from the plan cache. But plan_handle and sql_handle are opaque binary identifiers on their own; they don't tell you what the query actually says.

CROSS APPLY sys dot dm_exec_sql_text calls that function once per row, passing in that row's own sql_handle, and returns the actual T-SQL text. Run this during the mid-morning window, and one query rises to the top by a wide margin: Billing's invoice lookup, filtering dbo dot Invoices by PatientID. High execution count combined with high average logical reads is the specific signature of a query reading far more data than it needs.

Finding this query confirms Billing's complaint has a specific, identifiable cause. But it does not explain Scheduling's complaint. Nothing in this query touches dbo dot Appointments at all — the first real evidence that this investigation may turn up more than one root cause, exactly as Lesson 2 anticipated.
Next lesson reads this exact query's execution plan to see precisely what it's doing wrong — not guessing, but reading the real graphical plan the way a DBA does under pressure.
